title: Vipassana, insight
hook: an itch on the nose, watched instead of scratched: insight practice looks closely at change

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: satipatthana, a map with four places to look. Your line was four foundations.

An itch. Right on the side of the nose, in the middle of a quiet sit. The hand is already half-raised. Now a different move: the hand stays down, and the attention goes in close. A point, or a patch? Sharp, or buzzing? Steady, or pulsing? Watched like that, an itch tends to stop being one solid thing. It flickers. It moves. Sometimes it fades on its own, sometimes it flares and then fades. That small experiment, looking closely instead of reacting, is the heart of a whole school of practice.
screen: `AN ITCH, MID-SIT.` → `LOOK CLOSER, DON'T SCRATCH.` → `IT FLICKERS, IT MOVES.`

segments.voice: Vipassana is the Pali word usually translated insight. In Theravada practice, it means looking closely at experience until three things show themselves. First, change: in Pali, anicca. Sensations, moods, thoughts: watched closely, none of them holds still. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in four words: "All created things perish." Insight practice isn't about agreeing with that sentence. It's about seeing it happen, in an itch, a breath, a mood that was here a minute ago. Second, unsatisfactoriness: in Pali, dukkha. Because things keep changing, holding on to them is stressful. The pleasant sensation slips away; the hand tightens to keep it. Teachers point out that the strain is in the grabbing, not the changing. Third, not-self: in Pali, anatta. The itch arrived without permission. The thought showed up uninvited. Watched closely, experience seems to run along without a little manager inside approving each piece. The Buddha's teaching, as the Theravada schools pass it on, is that none of it can be held as me or mine. The Dhammapada places these three side by side and says seeing them is a way to purity. Fourth, why it's a practice and not a philosophy. Anyone can read that things change. Insight is the shift from knowing it in your head to watching it in your body, until the knowing changes how you hold things. Yesterday's four foundations are the places to look; vipassana is what the looking is for.
screen: `ONE: CHANGE, ANICCA.` · `TWO: THE STRAIN OF HOLDING ON, DUKKHA.` · `THREE: NOT-SELF, ANATTA.` · `FROM KNOWING IT TO SEEING IT.`

segments.voice: Let your attention find one sensation, an itch if there is one, or the touch of your hands, a warm spot, the pressure where you sit, and go in close: does it have edges, does it hold still, or flicker, fade and return? When it fades, find the next one, no need to name anything; if you need to move or scratch, notice the urge first, then move slowly.
Vipassana. Insight. Looking closely at experience until change, strain and not-self show themselves directly. Today's word.
Your line: watch it change. Even what seems solid tends to flicker when you look closely. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada insight meditation, practitioners sit and walk while watching sensations, thoughts and moods closely, looking for change, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in direct experience.

notes: Quoted Müller's Dhammapada 277 opening: 'All created things perish' (in Müller it sits inside single quotation marks). Confirm exact wording. Verses 278–279 (sorrow/pain and unreality/not-self) are paraphrased, not quoted.
Müller renders the three verses with 'created things' and 'forms'; the script uses the standard Pali terms anicca, dukkha, anatta for the three marks. Confirm the pairing to verses 277–279 is fair.
'none of it can be held as me or mine' summarizes the not-self teaching as Theravada passes it on; confirm phrasing.
The itch description is framed as what 'tends' to happen, not as what the listener will feel.
